section.title: It Is Good to Praise the Lord
section.sectionRationale: The only psalm titled explicitly for the Sabbath, this song contrasts the brief flourishing of the wicked, who sprout like grass only to be destroyed, with the righteous, who are planted in the house of the LORD and flourish even in old age, a truth resting finally on Christ, the Rock in whom there is no unrighteousness.
section.thesis: It is good to praise the LORD morning and night for His great works, trusting that though the wicked flourish briefly like grass, the righteous, planted in God's house, will bear fruit even in old age, a flourishing rooted in Christ the Rock, in whom there is no unrighteousness.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the call to praise God morning and night, verses 1-3; joy in the greatness of God's works, verses 4-5; the certain, sudden end of the wicked, verses 6-9; the vindication and anointing of the righteous, verses 10-11; and the righteous flourishing like a palm tree in God's house, verses 12-15.

units.label: Morning and Night Praise
units.note: the call to praise on the Sabbath

verses.text: It is good to praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name, O {{elyon|Most High}},
to proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning and Your faithfulness at night
with the ten-stringed harp and the melody of the lyre.

units.label: How Great Are Your Works
units.note: joy in the greatness of God's works

verses.text: For You, O LORD, have made me glad by Your deeds; I sing for joy at the works of Your hands.
How great are Your works, O LORD, how deep are Your thoughts!

units.label: They Will Be Forever Destroyed
units.note: the certain, sudden end of the wicked

verses.text: A senseless man does not know, and a fool does not understand,
that though the wicked sprout like grass, and all evildoers flourish, they will be forever destroyed.
But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!
For surely Your enemies, O LORD, surely Your enemies will perish; all evildoers will be scattered.
But You have exalted my horn like that of a wild ox; with fine oil I have been anointed.
My eyes see the downfall of my enemies; my ears hear the wailing of my wicked foes.

units.label: Flourishing Like a Palm Tree
units.note: the righteous planted in God's house

verses.text: The {{tsaddik|righteous}} will flourish like a {{tamar|palm tree}}, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
Planted in the house of the LORD, they will flourish in the courts of our God.
In old age they will still bear fruit; healthy and green they will remain,
to proclaim, "The LORD is upright; He is my {{tsur|Rock}}, and in Him there is no unrighteousness."

tsaddik.gloss: Righteous, one who is just or in right standing. The psalm pictures such a person not as flawless in themselves but as one rooted, planted, and dependent on the LORD for their flourishing.

tamar.gloss: A palm tree, known in Israel for its long life and continued fruitfulness even into great age, a fitting picture of the enduring vitality God grants the righteous.

elyon.gloss: Most High, a divine title emphasizing God's supremacy over every rival power. The psalm's opening call to praise is addressed directly to God under this exalted name.

tsur.gloss: Rock, a picture of stability, refuge, and unshakeable strength. The psalm closes by naming the LORD this Rock, in whom there is no unrighteousness, a title the New Testament applies to Christ.

basic.context: Titled a song for the Sabbath day, this psalm calls worshipers to praise God morning and night with music, then contrasts the wicked, who sprout quickly like grass only to be destroyed, with the righteous, who are planted in God's house and flourish with fruit even into old age.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes a real, lived contrast between the fleeting prosperity of the wicked and the rooted flourishing of the righteous, and it prescribes an abiding pattern of worship, marking every day, and especially the Sabbath, with deliberate praise for God's works.
basic.originalLanguages: This shabbat, Sabbath, song calls the tsaddik, righteous, verse 12, to flourish like a tamar, palm tree, known for bearing fruit even in old age, and closes by naming the LORD as tsur, Rock, verse 15, the foundation of stability in whom there is no unrighteousness.
basic.typology: The righteous 'planted in the house of the LORD,' verse 13, anticipates believers as living stones built into a spiritual house, and the psalm's closing title, 'the Rock,' points forward to Christ, the spiritual Rock from which His people drink.
basic.christ: Paul identifies the Rock that accompanied Israel as Christ Himself, 1 Corinthians 10:4, and this psalm's closing confession, 'He is my Rock, and in Him there is no unrighteousness,' finds its fullest truth in Jesus, the only truly righteous Rock on whom His people's flourishing depends.
basic.god: God is shown as the one whose works are great and whose thoughts are deep beyond the fool's understanding, exalted forever above every enemy, and faithful to make the righteous flourish and endure precisely because they are rooted in Him rather than in themselves.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 10:4 names Christ as the spiritual Rock. 1 Peter 2:5 describes believers as living stones built into a spiritual house. Hebrews 4:9-10 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, fulfilled in Christ.
basic.oneStory: This Sabbath song's contrast between the fleeting wicked and the enduringly fruitful righteous, planted in God's house and resting on Him as their Rock, points forward to Christ, the true Rock in whom believers are planted and in whom alone there is no unrighteousness.

context.literary:
Psalm 92 is built in three blocks, and the way they are balanced tells the reader where to look. The first block, verses 1 to 5, is praise and its reason. The second, verses 6 to 9, is about the wicked and the fool. The third, verses 10 to 15, is about the righteous. In the English text of fifteen verses the middle falls on verse 8: "But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!" It is the one line in the psalm that is about God alone, with no person, good or bad, in it, and it stands between the two human destinies like a stone between two streams. The name of the LORD occurs seven times in the psalm, in verses 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 13 and 15, and the Most High and our God are named as well.

The psalm is built on contrasts of time. It begins with the arc of a day, "in the morning" and "at night," verse 2, and it ends with the arc of a life, "in old age they will still bear fruit," verse 14. In between it sets a fast-growing thing against a slow one. The wicked "sprout like grass," and grass is up in days and gone in weeks, verse 7. The righteous "flourish like a palm tree" and "grow like a cedar," trees that take decades to stand and then stand for generations, verse 12. Even the verbs are meant to be heard together. The word that says the wicked sprout in verse 7 is the same verb that says the righteous flourish in verse 12, so that the contrast lies in the roots and not in the bloom.

The psalm also opens and closes with the same act. The worshiper resolves to "proclaim" God's loving devotion in verse 2, and the old fruitful trees are said "to proclaim" in verse 15 that the LORD is upright. What begins as a morning song becomes what a lifetime of fruit is for. The last word of the psalm is a short creed, "He is my Rock, and in Him there is no unrighteousness," and the whole poem exists to lead to that line.
context.historical:
The heading calls the psalm "a song for the Sabbath day," and it is the only psalm in the Psalter with that heading. The Sabbath was the seventh day that God had blessed and set apart at creation, Genesis 2:2-3, and it was given to Israel as a commandment in both forms of the Decalogue, with creation as the reason in Exodus 20:8-11 and the exodus as the reason in Deuteronomy 5:12-15. On that day the temple added its own offering, two lambs with grain and a drink offering, Numbers 28:9-10. The Levitical singers were accustomed to begin their song when the burnt offering began, with their instruments, as in Hezekiah's time, 2 Chronicles 29:27-28. The "ten-stringed harp" and the lyre of verse 3 belong to that world. Jewish tradition has sung this psalm on the Sabbath for centuries, in the temple service and in the synagogue.

The imagery of trees has a setting that Israel's first hearers would have known. The date palm grew thick in the Jordan valley, and Jericho was called "the City of Palms," Deuteronomy 34:3. The cedars of Lebanon were famed for their height and were cut for Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 5:6. Most telling, the walls of the temple were carved with "cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers," 1 Kings 6:29. To be "planted in the house of the LORD" was to stand among the living palms of the sanctuary walls, and another psalmist says, "I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God," Psalm 52:8.

The ox of verse 10 was a picture of wild, dangerous strength, and Israel sang that God had brought them out of Egypt "with strength like a wild ox," Numbers 23:22. Oil was poured on kings and priests and on honoured guests, Psalm 23:5. The problem the psalm takes up, why the wicked seem to flourish, was a live question in Israel's wisdom writers, as in Psalm 37, Psalm 73 and Job 21:7-9, and this psalm speaks as someone who has come through it.
context.canonical:
Psalm 92 sits between two other psalms that shape it. Psalm 90 is Moses' prayer that God would "satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion" and would make His people glad for as many days as they had been afflicted, Psalm 90:14-15. Psalm 92 answers with nearly the same words: "to proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning," verse 2, and "You, O LORD, have made me glad by Your deeds," verse 4. The grass that withered in Psalm 90:5-6 shows up again in verse 7 as the image of the wicked. Psalm 93, which follows, declares "The LORD reigns," and Psalm 92's central line, "You, O LORD, are exalted forever," points ahead to it.

The image of the planted tree is at home across the Old Testament. Psalm 1:3 says the man who delights in the law is "like a tree planted by streams of water," and Jeremiah 17:7-8 says the same of the one who trusts in the LORD. Isaiah 61:3 gives the tree a name: "oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified." The psalm's last line also echoes Moses' song. Deuteronomy 32:4 calls God "the Rock," "righteous and upright," "without injustice," and Psalm 92:15 is nearly that verse in a worshiper's mouth. Isaiah 46:4, "Even to your old age, I will be the same," is God's own promise behind verse 14.

In the New Testament the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ. Jesus is "Lord even of the Sabbath," Mark 2:28, and invites the weary to come and find rest, Matthew 11:28-30. Hebrews says "there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God," Hebrews 4:9, and Colossians calls the Sabbath a shadow whose body belongs to Christ, Colossians 2:16-17. Paul identifies the Rock as Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4, and Jesus' picture of His people as branches that bear much fruit, John 15:1-8, is the planted tree of the psalm given a person to grow in.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wrote to help worshipers see through the noise of a world in which the wicked often look like they are winning. The psalm does not argue the point with statistics. It sets out a pattern of worship that makes the truth visible. You start the day and end the night with praise, you look at what God has made and what He has done, and you come to see that He is greater than the things you feared. The "fool" of verse 6 fails to understand because he has no place to stand from which to see, while the worshiper sees from inside the house of the LORD, where the end of the wicked can be read. Psalm 73:17 says the same: "until I entered God's sanctuary; then I discerned their end."

The author also wanted to put a picture of a good life in front of God's people: not a life of quick success, but a rooted one, green and fruitful to the end. The measure of that life is what it does with its years, which is to keep declaring that God is upright. It is a Sabbath song because the Sabbath is when a people stop working long enough to look at what God has done and to be glad in it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a pattern that holds in God's world and does not offer a guarantee for each person. Verses 7 and 12 to 14 speak in general terms about the wicked and the righteous. The Bible itself records exceptions: Job suffered, the psalmist of Psalm 73 nearly lost his footing, and Barzillai at eighty could no longer taste his food, 2 Samuel 19:35. The psalm does not promise that every believer will be robust at ninety. The fruit of verse 14 is what verse 15 says it is, a proclamation that the LORD is upright, and that can be borne by a person in a wheelchair as well as by one who runs.

Verses 10 and 11 describe how one person experienced the fall of enemies. They do not prescribe a taste for revenge, and Proverbs 24:17 forbids gloating over an enemy's fall. What the psalm prescribes is the rhythm of worship. The believer is to make it good to praise, to do so at the start and end of each day, and to pause for it on the day God set apart. It also invites the people of God to put themselves down in the place of worship, because trees that are planted there flourish.

debates.question: Does verse 7's promise that the wicked 'will be forever destroyed' describe a specific historical judgment or a final, eschatological one?

views.label: It primarily describes the recurring pattern of temporal judgment on the wicked within history
views.case: The surrounding wisdom language, comparing the wicked to quickly sprouting grass, echoes Psalm 37 and 73's observations about the fleeting nature of wicked prosperity within ordinary life and history.

views.label: It points forward to final, eschatological judgment and destruction
views.case: The absolute language, 'forever destroyed,' paired with the LORD being 'exalted forever,' verse 8, suggests a judgment as permanent and complete as God's own eternal reign, pointing beyond any single historical downfall.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that present appearances are deceptive, wicked flourishing is always temporary, and the righteous can trust God's justice whether it unfolds within history or is completed only at the final judgment.

debates.question: Who is the 'I' of verses 10 and 11?

views.label: A king
views.case: The raised horn and the anointing oil are royal images, and the enemies of verse 11 are the kind a king faces. Psalm 132:17 speaks of a horn growing for David, and Samuel anointed David with a horn of oil, 1 Samuel 16:13. On this view the psalm is a king's thanksgiving that Israel sang on his behalf.

views.label: Any worshiper
views.case: The psalm has been a Sabbath song for the whole congregation, and verse 4 speaks as one who has been made glad by God's works. Oil was also poured on honoured guests, Psalm 23:5, so 'anointed' may mean that God has lifted up and refreshed the speaker. The BSB note on verse 11 offers 'my ears hear evildoers when they rise against me,' which keeps the enemies closer to ordinary life.

views.label: A king who speaks for the people
views.case: The king's victory and the congregation's confidence are treated as one in Israel's worship. The 'I' may be a king, and the people sing it as theirs because his standing is theirs.

debates.bearing: The second and third views suit the psalm's plain use as a Sabbath song. They also leave room for the royal colouring to point to the Anointed One, who stands for His people and whose triumph they share.

debates.question: What becomes of the Sabbath in the light of Christ?

views.label: It continues on the seventh day
views.case: The Sabbath was blessed at creation and set in the Ten Commandments, and Jesus said it was 'made for man,' Mark 2:27. On this view the day still stands, and Christians should honour it as Israel did.

views.label: It continues on the Lord's day
views.case: The first Christians met on the first day of the week, Acts 20:7, and John calls it 'the Lord's day,' Revelation 1:10. Many Reformed and Puritan writers held that the principle of one day in seven was carried over to Sunday.

views.label: It is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the rest it pointed to
views.case: Colossians 2:16-17 calls the Sabbath a shadow whose body belongs to Christ, and Hebrews 4:9-10 speaks of a rest still to be entered by faith. On this view the church keeps a rhythm of rest and worship freely, and no one may judge another about a day.

debates.bearing: Psalm 92 gives all three a common ground. Its Sabbath is a day for praise, gladness and proclamation, and not only for stopping work. Isaiah 58:13-14 says the same: call it 'a delight.' Whatever day a believer keeps, this is what the day is for.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm opens with "good," and then gives two verbs of praise that are worth telling apart. "To praise" in verse 1 is from yadah, which means to acknowledge or confess, and it is used of thanking God for what He has done. "To sing praises" is from zamar, to make music, which gives the psalm its name, mizmor. The first is praise with the mouth and the second is praise with the instruments, and verse 3 names three of them: a ten-stringed instrument, the harp and the lyre. The last is called by a word, higgayon, that elsewhere means meditation, as in Psalm 19:14, "the meditation of my heart." The melody on the lyre is named for meditation, which suggests a reflective sound.

The word for "thoughts" in verse 5, machshevotekha, covers God's plans and purposes, and the word "deep" is a word for a depth that cannot be seen to the bottom. Together they say the same thing that Isaiah does when God declares that His thoughts are higher than ours, Isaiah 55:8-9, and that Paul does in the cry "How unsearchable are His judgments," Romans 11:33.

Verse 6 names two kinds of people who fail to see. The "senseless man" is ba'ar, from the word for a brute animal, and it is the word the psalmist of Psalm 73:22 uses of himself when he confesses, "I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You." The "fool" is kesil, the person in Proverbs who will not be taught. The first has lost his reason, and the second refuses instruction.

The pivotal verb is parach, to sprout or blossom. It appears of the wicked in verse 7, "the wicked sprout like grass," and of the righteous in verse 12, "will flourish like a palm tree." It is the verb used of Aaron's staff that budded, Numbers 17:8. The same act of springing up is the thing both groups do, and the difference lies in what they are rooted in.

In verse 13 "planted" comes from a verb that means transplanted, a tree set deliberately in a chosen place, and the same form describes the tree of Psalm 1:3 and Jeremiah 17:8. The righteous are not an accident of the soil. They were put where they are.

Verse 10's "fine oil" translates a word for fresh, green, luxuriant, ra'anan, and verse 14 uses the same root of the old who stay "green," so that the anointing at the start and the green old age at the end are related. The word for "old age," seivah, is literally grey hair, and the verb "bear fruit" is one that describes yield. God's oil and God's greenness are one gift.

The last verse's word "unrighteousness" is a word for injustice or crookedness from the root behind "without injustice" in Deuteronomy 32:4. The psalm has taken the closing statement of Moses' song about the Rock and made it the closing statement of every old tree.

typology.type: The Sabbath rest, the day of the psalm
typology.fulfillment: The Sabbath of creation, Genesis 2:2-3, and the Sabbath of the commandment, Exodus 20:8-11, looked beyond themselves to a rest that God's people would share with Him. Jesus claims it as His own: 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28, and He is 'Lord even of the Sabbath,' Mark 2:28. Hebrews says that whoever enters God's rest 'rests from his own work, just as God did from His,' Hebrews 4:10. Colossians calls the Sabbath 'a shadow of the things to come,' Colossians 2:17. The type is partly kept and partly waiting, for the full rest still lies ahead.

typology.type: Planted in the house of the LORD, Psalm 92:13
typology.fulfillment: The trees of verse 13 are planted in the sanctuary, where palms were carved on the walls, 1 Kings 6:29. Paul and Peter use building language of the church: 'in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22, and 'like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house,' 1 Peter 2:5. The people are no longer planted in a building but become the building, because Christ is its cornerstone. The escalation is that God's house no longer has a courtyard to stand outside. The picture of a tree is also kept, for Jesus says, 'Remain in Me, and I will remain in you,' John 15:4.

typology.type: The anointed one with the raised horn, Psalm 92:10
typology.fulfillment: The horn lifted high and the oil poured out are royal marks, and the title Christ means Anointed One. Zechariah sings that God 'has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69. Jesus reads Isaiah in the synagogue, 'The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me,' Luke 4:18, and Peter says 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power,' Acts 10:38. The anointing is also shared: 'It is God who establishes both us and you in Christ. He anointed us,' 2 Corinthians 1:21. The type is uncertain in its first reference, since the psalm does not name a king, so it is an echo and not a declared prophecy.

typology.type: The Rock in whom there is no injustice, Psalm 92:15
typology.fulfillment: Moses called the LORD 'the Rock,' Deuteronomy 32:4, and the psalm closes by making the same confession. Paul says of the wilderness generation, 'they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. The correspondence is that the Rock Israel leaned on in every trial was the pre-incarnate Son. Jesus also says that the one who hears His words and does them is like a wise man who built on the rock, Matthew 7:24. The type deepens because the Rock who is without injustice takes on flesh and dies for the unjust, 1 Peter 3:18.

The palm that stands for the flourishing righteous turns up in the palm branches that crowds wave for the coming King, John 12:13, and in the vision of the multitude before the throne 'holding palm branches in their hands,' Revelation 7:9. This is an echo and not a fulfilment the New Testament declares, but the pattern is clear. The palm belongs to the victory of the righteous, and the righteous in the end are those who stand with the Lamb. The correspondence breaks in that the Jerusalem crowd's palms wilted in days, while the palms of Revelation belong to a people who do not fade.

study.christ:
Psalm 92 leads to Christ in five ways, and all of them hold because the psalm is about a God who is praised for His works and trusted for His uprightness.

First, through the Sabbath. The song was written for the day on which Israel stopped work to rejoice in what God had made, and the Gospels show Jesus at the centre of that day. He heals on the Sabbath and answers His critics, "To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working," and claims to be "Lord even of the Sabbath," John 5:17 and Mark 2:28. The psalm's joy in the works of God's hands, verse 4, becomes in the Gospels the works of the Son, "so that the works of God would be displayed," John 9:3. The rest the psalm's day pointed to is what Jesus offers: "I will give you rest," Matthew 11:28. On the cross He says "It is finished," John 19:30, and the work that gave the original Sabbath its meaning is gathered up in it.

Second, through the Anointed One. The oil of verse 10 belongs to kings and priests, and Jesus is the Anointed in the fullest sense. He reads Isaiah's words, "The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me," Luke 4:18, and is called the horn of salvation, Luke 1:69. The enemies whose downfall the psalm sees are the powers He has disarmed, Colossians 2:15.

Third, through the Rock. The psalm ends by saying that the LORD is upright and that in Him there is no unrighteousness. No one fits that line more exactly than Jesus. He is the one who was "without sin," Hebrews 4:15, "the Holy and Righteous One," Acts 3:14, and He stands as "the righteous for the unrighteous," 1 Peter 3:18. Paul's statement that "the rock was Christ," 1 Corinthians 10:4, joins Israel's confession to Him by name.

Fourth, through fruit. The righteous flourish like palms and bear fruit even in old age. Jesus says, "I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit," John 15:5. He also shows the way fruit comes: "unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit," John 12:24. The long flourishing of the psalm is the flourishing of those who live in Him.

Fifth, through gladness. The psalmist is "made glad" by God's deeds. Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit and praised the Father, Luke 10:21, and He says He has spoken to His followers "so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete," John 15:11. The joy of a Sabbath psalm is a joy He shares.

A caution is needed. The psalm is not a prediction of Jesus, and most of its words are about Israel's worshiper and Israel's God. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of the Sabbath, the Rock, anointing and fruit, and do not treat every image in the psalm as a hidden picture of Him.
study.god:
Psalm 92 starts from a fact about God and builds a whole way of life on it: it is good to praise Him. The goodness is not in the feeling. It is in the fit. God is the kind of God whom it is right to praise, so that to praise Him is to see things as they are.

The God of this psalm is great in His works and deep in His thoughts, verse 5. His works are what He has done, and His thoughts are what He means by them. The worshiper can see the first and only glimpse the second, and that difference is the gap between the wise and the fool, verse 6. Paul stands at the same edge when he says "how unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways," Romans 11:33. God is not simple to read, and the right reaction is awe and not complaint.

He is exalted forever. Verse 8 is the only line in the psalm that speaks of God alone, and it is placed at the centre of the psalm. All the flourishing of the wicked and the triumph of the righteous happens around this fixed point. The psalm holds that His height is not a distance from human life. It is the place from which He sees and judges it.

He is just, and He is patient about it. The wicked sprout and appear to do well, but they are "forever destroyed," and His enemies "will perish," verses 7 and 9. The psalm does not claim that the end comes at once. It says it comes, and it gives the worshiper leave to wait. This fits what Psalm 73 says, that the end becomes plain to the one who enters God's sanctuary.

He is faithful from morning to night, in loving devotion and in faithfulness, verse 2. The two great attributes of His covenant name are matched to the two halves of the day, and the psalm implies that neither is ever off duty. He is also a God who sustains His people to the end. "Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray," Isaiah 46:4. The fruit in old age of verse 14 is His doing before it is theirs.

And He is upright. The psalm's last word calls Him a Rock, and the verse fills the word with two parts: He is upright, and there is no injustice in Him. A world in which the wicked flourish can make God seem unjust, and this line is the answer that the worshiper is sent out to proclaim.

He also rests. The Sabbath in the heading points to the God who, after the work of creation, "rested from all His work," Genesis 2:2-3, and who invites His people into a rest and delight of their own. For worship, the psalm teaches that praise is a duty and a pleasure, that it is best done in company and in the house of God, and that its content is the righteousness of the Lord who made the world and will set it right.

crossReferences.note: Moses prayed to be satisfied in the morning with God's loving devotion and to be made glad for as long as he had been afflicted. Psalm 92:2 and 92:4 use the same words of morning loving devotion and being made glad. The Sabbath song reads as the answer to the wilderness prayer.

The man who delights in God's law is a tree planted by streams, yielding fruit in season, and the wicked are chaff. Psalm 92 gives the same two fates and the same tree, now rooted in the house of the LORD and kept green into old age.

The one who trusts in the LORD is a tree planted by water that does not fear when heat comes and never stops bearing fruit. It is the same verb and image as Psalm 92:13, and it makes clear that the secret of the flourishing tree is where it is rooted.

David calls himself 'an olive tree flourishing in the house of God.' It is the nearest parallel to Psalm 92:13, and it shows that being planted in the sanctuary was a familiar picture of a believer who is secure and fruitful because he is near God.

The mourners of Zion are renamed 'oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified.' The psalm's tree is given a purpose. The righteous flourish so that God's glory is seen, which is what verse 15 says in proclaiming that He is upright.

The psalmist who nearly slipped over the prosperity of the wicked says that he understood their end only when he entered God's sanctuary. It is the experience behind Psalm 92:6 to 9, where the fool cannot see what the worshiper in God's house sees.

Moses calls God the Rock whose work is perfect, 'righteous and upright,' 'without injustice.' Psalm 92:15 is the same confession in a worshiper's voice, and it shows the psalm is carrying the last words of Moses into the Sabbath liturgy.

God promises to be the same to old age and to carry His people when they turn grey. It is the divine side of Psalm 92:14. The fruit that the old bear comes from a God who says 'I have made you, and I will carry you.'

The fourth commandment gives the Sabbath its ground in creation: six days of labour and a seventh day blessed and set apart. The psalm's title places its praise on that day, and the psalm's delight in God's works is the content of the rest.

A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters it rests from his own work as God did from His. The Sabbath song is read as a foretaste of what the writer says is still ahead, a rest entered by faith in Christ.

Paul says a Sabbath is a shadow of things to come and the body that casts it belongs to Christ. It shows how the psalm's day is taken up in the New Testament, not cancelled but fulfilled, with Christ as the reality the day pointed to.

Jesus is the true vine and His people are branches who bear much fruit if they remain in Him. It is the planted tree of the psalm given a Person to grow in, and the fruit that glorifies the Father is the flourishing the psalm promises to the righteous.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 92 is sung on the seventh day, and the seventh day is where the Bible's story starts. God finished His work, rested, and blessed and set apart the day, Genesis 2:2-3. Before there was sin or sorrow there was a Sabbath, a day in which humans shared in God's own delight in what He had made. The psalm is a song for that day. It restores the first human calling, to see God's works and to be glad in them.

The fall put a question across that calling. In a world under a curse the wicked sprout like grass and seem to do well, and the honest find it hard to see God's hand. The psalm is an answer from inside the question. The wicked are real, their prosperity is real, and so is their end. The righteous, meanwhile, are planted in the house of the LORD and keep green into old age. That is the same contrast the whole Old Testament draws between the two ways, from Psalm 1 to the wisdom books.

The psalm sits in the centre of a short arc in Book IV. Psalm 90 is a prayer under judgment. Psalm 92 is the morning that prayer asked for, and Psalm 93 follows with the declaration that the LORD reigns. Israel's own history then enacts the contrast. It is planted in a land and a temple, is uprooted in exile, and waits to be planted again, as Isaiah promises, as oaks of righteousness, Isaiah 61:3.

Christ is where the trees are planted for good. He is the Lord of the Sabbath who gives rest, the Anointed One whose horn is raised, the Rock without injustice, and the true vine in whom His people bear fruit. His resurrection is "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," 1 Corinthians 15:20, the first of a harvest that does not wither. The church lives in the meantime in a Sabbath that is both kept and still ahead, and Hebrews says it is waiting for the rest that remains.

The new creation is the psalm's day without end. A later Jewish tradition heard Psalm 92 as a song for the age to come, for the day that will be entirely Sabbath, and Revelation agrees with its direction. The tree of life is open and bears a fresh crop each month, and there is no longer any curse, Revelation 22:2-3. A multitude stands before the throne "holding palm branches in their hands," Revelation 7:9. The fool who could not see has been shown, the enemies have gone, and the righteous, planted in the courts of God, proclaim forever what the psalm's last line said: the LORD is upright, He is our Rock, and in Him there is no unrighteousness.

quiz.q: What is this psalm uniquely titled for, according to its heading?

options.text: A song for the Sabbath day.
options.note: Psalm 92 is the only psalm in the Psalter explicitly titled for the Sabbath.

options.text: A song for a coronation.
options.note: The heading names the Sabbath, not a coronation, as the occasion.

options.text: A song for a funeral.
options.note: The psalm's tone is joyful praise, not funeral lament.

options.text: A song of general praise and thanksgiving to God.
options.note: This is true of its content and tone, but the heading specifically names the Sabbath day as its occasion, unique among all the psalms.

quiz.q: What comparison does verse 7 use to describe the wicked?

options.text: They sprout like grass and flourish briefly, but will be forever destroyed.
options.note: The verse contrasts the wicked's quick, temporary flourishing with their certain, lasting destruction.

options.text: They are like cedar trees that last for centuries.
options.note: Cedar imagery in this psalm describes the righteous, not the wicked.

options.text: They never experience any success at all.
options.note: The verse acknowledges the wicked do flourish, though only briefly.

options.text: They prosper for a season but face inevitable decline.
options.note: This is essentially correct in substance, though the verse's specific and vivid image is grass that sprouts quickly and is just as quickly destroyed forever.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the righteous in verses 12-14?

options.text: Flourishing like a palm tree, planted in God's house, bearing fruit even in old age.
options.note: These verses picture enduring vitality and fruitfulness rooted in being planted in the LORD's house.

options.text: Withering quickly like grass.
options.note: That description belongs to the wicked, not the righteous, in this psalm.

options.text: Flourishing only in youth, then fading entirely.
options.note: The psalm specifically says the righteous still bear fruit in old age.

options.text: Growing strong and enduring like a great tree.
options.note: This is true and close to correct, but the psalm's fuller picture specifically names being planted in the house of the LORD as the source of that enduring strength.

quiz.q: What title does the psalm give the LORD in its closing verse?

options.text: My Rock, in whom there is no unrighteousness.
options.note: Verse 15 closes with this confession of God's uprightness and stability.

options.text: My enemy, to be feared and avoided.
options.note: The psalm's closing confession is one of trust and praise, not fear or avoidance.

options.text: A distant judge with no relationship to His people.
options.note: The title 'my Rock' expresses close, personal trust, not distance.

options.text: A God who is entirely just and reliable.
options.note: This is true and closely related, but the psalm's exact closing words specifically name Him 'my Rock,' emphasizing close, personal trust, not only abstract justice.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament connect to this psalm's closing image of the Rock?

options.text: Paul identifies Christ Himself as the spiritual Rock that accompanied Israel.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 10:4 names Christ as this Rock, fulfilling the psalm's closing confession.

options.text: The New Testament never uses rock imagery for God or Christ.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 10:4 explicitly uses this very image, applying it to Christ.

options.text: It connects only to a literal geological formation in Israel.
options.note: The connection is theological and christological, not merely geological.

options.text: It anticipates a sure foundation on which God's people can safely stand.
options.note: This is true in a general sense, but the precise New Testament connection is Paul's direct identification of Christ Himself as this spiritual Rock, 1 Corinthians 10:4.

questions: This psalm calls for praise both morning and night. What would it look like for you to deliberately mark the beginning and end of your day with praise to God?
The wicked are described as sprouting like grass, flourishing briefly before being destroyed. Have you ever envied the apparent, short-lived success of those who ignore God?
The righteous are pictured as planted in God's house, not growing on their own. Where do you tend to seek your own strength instead of staying rooted in God's presence and worship?
Verse 14 promises the righteous will still bear fruit in old age. How does this promise encourage you, whether you are early or late in life, about ongoing fruitfulness for God?
The psalm closes by calling God 'my Rock, in whom there is no unrighteousness.' How does trusting Christ as this Rock change the way you face uncertainty or temptation this week?

translationNotes.note: This is the only psalm in the Psalter explicitly titled 'A song for the Sabbath day,' and was read in Second Temple worship on the seventh day.
The horn exalted like a wild ox is an idiom for renewed strength and honor, and fine oil pictures anointing for blessing and joy.
The palm tree was valued in the ancient Near East for continuing to bear dates for many decades, making it a fitting image for enduring fruitfulness in old age.
